extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, petitioners, patent owners, USPTO staff involved in AIA trial proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for instituting and conducting post-grant reviews, inter partes reviews, and transitional covered business method (CBM) patent reviews under the AIA, including petition content, timing, discovery, claim construction, and pendency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation before issuing a stay affecting statutory deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: It is expected that the Director would be consulted prior to issuance of a stay, given that the stay would impact the ability of the Office to meet the statutory deadline for completing the post-grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: consult the Director before issuing a stay in an ex parte reexamination where the three-month statutory time period under 35 U.S.C. 303 is running.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder request deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner or petitioner may request a joinder, but such a request must be filed no later than one month after institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section reference: § 42.222(b). The Board may adjust the one-year scheduling in the case of joinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental information post-institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplemental information identified in motions must be filed after the institution of the post-grant review because institution is based on information in the petition and any response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory basis: 35 U.S.C. 326(a)(3) and 35 U.S.C. 324(a). Motions identifying supplemental information are to be filed after institution; supplemental info is not the basis for institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and standard for additional discovery in post-grant review
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional discovery is limited to evidence directly related to factual assertions advanced by a party to the proceeding, and the standard for additional discovery is good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with 35 U.S.C. 326(a)(5). Good cause requires a specific factual reason to justify needed discovery; additional discovery should be tailored to facts in dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different discovery standards across proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-grant reviews (and covered business method reviews) employ a 'good cause' standard for additional discovery, whereas inter partes reviews and derivation proceedings use an 'interests-of-justice' standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interests-of-justice is a slightly higher standard than good cause and considers broader factors and 'totality of the relevant circumstances' (U.S. v. Roberts). Good cause focuses on specific factual justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: CBM review as trial subject to subpart rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered business method patent review is a trial and subject to the rules set forth in subpart A and to post-grant review procedures in subpart C, except for specified sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.300(a). CBM is regarded as, and shall employ standards and procedures of, a post-grant review with certain enumerated exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard: broadest reasonable interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim in an unexpired patent shall be given its broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification in which it appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.300(b) and related: consistent with 35 U.S.C. 326 and longstanding USPTO practice (e.g., Yamamoto). Justifications include ability to amend claims, preponderance standard, absence of presumption of validity, and consistency across merged proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-year pendency with possible six-month extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings are to be administered within a one-year timeframe after institution, with a six-month extension available for good cause; the one-year period may be adjusted in the case of joinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with 35 U.S.C. 326(a)(11). Extensions are anticipated to be rare; whether good cause exists depends on particular facts (example: new evidence uncovered late necessitating motion to amend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal effect of CBM rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules in subpart D are in effect until September 15, 2020, except they continue to apply to any CBM review filed before the date of repeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent with AIA section 18(a)(3)(A)–(B); transitional program sunset provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may petition for CBM review (standing requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may not file a petition for CBM review unless the petitioner, its real party-in-interest, or a privy of the petitioner has been sued for infringement or has been charged with infringement under that patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.302(a). 'Charged with infringement' is defined as a real and substantial controversy such that petitioner would have standing to bring a declaratory judgment action in Federal court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel bar for CBM petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner (or its real party-in-interest or privy) may not file a petition for CBM review where that party is estopped from challenging the claims on the grounds identified in the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.302(b). Consistent with 35 U.S.C. 325(e)(1) estoppel provisions based on final written decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing restriction for CBM petitions relative to PGR
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for CBM review may be filed at any time except during the period in which a petition for post-grant review of the patent would satisfy the statutory nine-month restriction (35 U.S.C. 321(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.303 and AIA section 18(a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition must demonstrate standing and CBM eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition must demonstrate that the petitioner has grounds for standing, certify that the patent is a covered business method patent, and show that the petitioner meets eligibility requirements of § 42.302.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.304(a). Facially improper standing can be a basis for denying a petition without reaching the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required contents of a petition (precise relief and specificity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition must identify each claim being challenged, the specific grounds on which each claim is challenged, how the claims are to be construed, why the claims as construed are unpatentable, and the exhibit numbers and portions of evidence relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.304(b) and 35 U.S.C. 322(a)(3)-(4). Purpose is to provide an efficient means to identify legal and factual bases supporting a prima facie case and to give the patent owner notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to correct clerical errors do not change filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner seeking to correct clerical or typographical mistakes may file a motion to correct them, but the grant of such a motion will not alter the filing date of the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.304(c). Filing date remains the original date for timeliness determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case approach to identifying real party-in-interest and privy
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations of 'real party-in-interest' and 'privy' are highly fact-dependent and will be made on a case-by-case basis using controlling case law and particular facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office will provide further guidance in the Patent Trial Practice Guide and through opinions and promptly publish relevant decisions. No rigid definitions in regulation due to fact dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for RPI/privy determinations including control
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may consider whether a non-party exercised or could have exercised control over a party’s participation in a proceeding and the degree of that control in determining RPI/privy status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other relevant factors may also be considered; Patent Trial Practice Guide discusses examples; Joint Defense Agreement membership alone does not automatically create RPI/privy status but is a relevant fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: When challenges to RPI identification must be filed
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges to 'real party-in-interest' identification should be brought before or with the filing of the patent owner preliminary response to give the Board time to decide before institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the preliminary response, likelihood of authorizing discovery related to the challenge decreases because the Board must decide institution within three months from filing of the patent owner preliminary response. Standing issues may still be raised during the trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update requirement for RPI changes
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must file an update within 21 days of a change to the 'real party-in-interest' identification; the Office generally accepts the petitioner's identification at filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 42.8(a)(3). Patent owner may present objective evidence in a preliminary response to challenge the identification; Board will consider such evidence when deciding whether to grant the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery to investigate RPI identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional discovery may be authorized where a patent owner raises sufficient concerns regarding the petitioner's certification of real party-in-interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board can authorize pertinent discovery, particularly when a challenge is raised before or with the preliminary response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for willful misrepresentation regarding petitioner status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has discretion to impose appropriate sanctions against a party for misconduct, such as willfully misleading the Office about being a proper petitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depending on facts including intent to misrepresent, sanctions may be imposed; see § 42.12 for misconduct provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: High threshold and rarity for one-year extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensions of the one-year period are anticipated to be rare; a high threshold for granting extension (good cause) is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether good cause is shown depends on particular facts (e.g., late-discovered evidence necessitating motion to amend). Sections 42.100(c) and 42.200(c) implement the one-year rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and Board jurisdiction if one-year period missed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office does not envision extending reviews beyond the statutory time periods and has not articulated a general recourse if the Board misses the one-year period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory scheme (35 U.S.C. 316(a)(11), 326(a)(11)) requires final determinations within one year (extendable six months for good cause); the Office currently expects to meet these timeframes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustments for foreign parties and scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may consider any factor that might affect ability to meet the one-year period and adjust the schedule accordingly, including providing less time for judicial deliberations for parties outside the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board has discretion to accommodate circumstances that affect schedule while still aiming to meet statutory deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and authorization for motions to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners must seek authorization to file a motion to amend claims after a patent owner response; late motions may be denied to preserve ability to complete the proceeding within the one-year period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 42.121 and 42.221 require authorization so Board can determine proper scheduling and possibly deny late motions that would impede timely completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory timing for filing post-grant review petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for post-grant review must be filed within the time period required by statute (nine months from issuance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 321(c) sets the nine-month requirement; nine months is the statutory requirement and cannot be shortened by rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing IPR when PGR institution decision pending
rubrics_metrics.description: If nine months have passed since issuance but no decision on whether to institute a post-grant review has been entered, a party may file a petition for inter partes review without waiting for the institution decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses timing conflicts between PGR and IPR filing windows; statutory language allows filing after later of nine months or termination of instituted PGR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting number of petitions not anticipated currently
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Director has authority to limit number of petitions, the Office does not plan to limit the number of petitions at this time; if a limit were imposed, petitions filed after the limit would be considered untimely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 6(c)(2)(B) and 6(f)(2)(B) of AIA allow limits on a yearly basis; any future limit would be accompanied by notice and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition fees set with consideration of aggregate cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition fees have been set with consideration for the aggregate cost of the proceeding to help the Office provide necessary resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 321(a) and fee-setting rationale: fees are intended to allow Office to handle demand without limiting petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping of claims in petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners may group claims where the basis for alleged unpatentability of grouped claims is the same, but must provide sufficient notice as to the merits of the challenge for each claim so challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouping is permitted, but the petition still must provide specific reasoning and evidence tying the ground to each claim in the group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and evidentiary sufficiency in petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Petition must set forth a full statement of the reasons for the relief requested, including a detailed explanation of the significance of the evidence, specify where each claim element is found in prior art, and provide specific citations to the evidence; corroborating evidence must be included if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 41.22(a)(3), 41.104, and 41.204 require detail sufficient to meet statutory grounds for unpatentability and to establish a prima facie case; where corroboration is necessary (e.g., on-sale/public use), include it with the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction uniformity across merged proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim construction standard (broadest reasonable interpretation) must be used throughout a proceeding reviewing patentability, including any new or amended claims and claims from merged proceedings (reexamination, reissue, derivation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids inconsistencies and inefficiencies; historical USPTO and Federal Circuit practice supports broadest reasonable interpretation in Office patentability proceedings.
